title: Three-element Yagi antenna for VHF and UHF radios
summary: A simple directional antenna that roughly triples a handheld radio's effective power in the direction you point it, and cuts noise from other directions. Build it from aluminium rod, tube or steel tape measure on a wooden or plastic boom, cut to lengths worked out for your frequency.

materials.item: Elements: aluminium rod or tube 3–10 mm, stiff copper wire, or a 25 mm steel tape measure
materials.qty: about 3 m for the 2 m band, 1 m for UHF

materials.item: Boom: dry wood or plastic pipe, 20–40 mm
materials.qty: 0.5 m longer than the element spacing

materials.item: 50 Ω coax with a connector to fit your radio
Hose clamps, screws or zip ties to fix elements
Mast: wooden pole or steel tube
Tape and sealant for the feed point

steps.text: Pick the frequency you use most and work out the element lengths and spacings from the table or formula in the notes.
Cut the boom: total spacing plus about 10 cm at each end. Mark where each element goes.
Cut the reflector and director to length from rod or tape. Cut the driven element as two equal halves, leaving a 10–20 mm gap between them at the centre.
steps.warn: Cut tape-measure and sheet edges are sharp. File the ends and cover them with tape.

steps.text: Fix the elements across the boom at the marks, all parallel and centred: reflector at the back, driven element, director at the front. On a wooden or plastic boom they can pass straight through or clamp on top.
Connect the coax at the gap: centre conductor to one half of the driven element, braid to the other half. Keep the unshielded ends as short as possible.
Coil 5–8 turns of the coax into a loop about 10–15 cm across right next to the feed point and tape it. This choke keeps signal off the outside of the coax.
Seal the feed point against rain with tape and sealant; water inside coax ruins it.

Tune: with an SWR meter, trim the driven element ends a few millimetres at a time until SWR is lowest at your frequency. Without one, test with a friend several kilometres away and compare with your normal antenna.
Mount the antenna on a mast, elements vertical for handheld FM radios, director pointing at the other station. Run the coax down with a few loose loops.
steps.warn: Keep the mast and antenna well away from overhead power lines: falling into one kills. Work on ladders with a second person.

steps.text: To find a station, turn the antenna slowly and listen for the strongest signal. Height gains more range than anything else.

notes:
## Dimensions
Wavelength λ (mm) = 300,000 ÷ frequency (MHz).
- Reflector: 0.495 λ
- Driven element (tip to tip, including gap): 0.473 λ
- Director: 0.440 λ
- Reflector to driven element: 0.20 λ
- Driven element to director: 0.15 λ

| Use | MHz | Reflector | Driven | Director | R–D spacing | D–Dir spacing |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 m amateur | 146 | 1,017 mm | 972 mm | 904 mm | 411 mm | 308 mm |
| Marine VHF | 156.8 | 947 mm | 905 mm | 842 mm | 383 mm | 287 mm |
| PMR446 | 446 | 333 mm | 318 mm | 296 mm | 135 mm | 101 mm |
| FRS/GMRS | 462 | 321 mm | 307 mm | 286 mm | 130 mm | 97 mm |

Thick elements (tape measure, wide tube) act a little longer; cut the driven element 1–2% long and trim to tune.

## Matching
This antenna's feed impedance is about 20–30 Ω, so straight 50 Ω coax gives an SWR of about 2:1. That's acceptable at handheld powers (5W or less). For a better match, add a hairpin: a U-shaped loop of stiff wire across the feed gap, 3–10 cm long, adjusted with an SWR meter.

## What you gain
A 3-element Yagi gives about 5 dB over a simple dipole: roughly 3× the power in the direction it points, and less noise from behind. In open country that may add roughly 50–80% to range. Height matters more.

## Height and line of sight
VHF and UHF travel roughly line of sight. Radio horizon (km) ≈ 4.1 × (√h1 + √h2), heights in metres. Two handhelds at 2 m: about 12 km over flat ground. One antenna raised to 10 m: about 19 km. Hills block signal; get above them.

## Polarisation
Both stations must match. Handheld FM radios are vertical, so mount elements vertical. Horizontal is used for long-distance SSB and TV.

## Rules and safety
In normal times, licence rules may limit antennas on licence-free radios (PMR446, FRS) and require a licence for amateur bands. Don't stand right in front of a Yagi when transmitting at high power (above about 25W). At handheld power it's not a concern.

## Receive-only uses
Point it at a distant repeater, weather broadcast, or emergency channel to pull in weak signals on a scanner.

## Wi-Fi
At 2.4 GHz elements are about 6 cm long and need millimetre accuracy. A salvaged satellite dish with a small feed at its focus is easier and gives more gain.

## If you lack a part
- No aluminium: steel tape measure, stiff copper wire, welding rod, or brazing rod all work.
- No coax: twin-lead cable fed straight to the gap works at short runs but picks up noise; keep it under a few metres.

sources.title: Standard 3-element Yagi proportions from amateur radio practice
